deck.headline: Anthropic closes its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, valuing it near $1.8 trillion
deck.sub: ANT touched $115 in early Nasdaq trading before fading as the wider tech market fell 2.3%; after hours it slipped to about $92.
deck.summary: Anthropic's shares closed their first Nasdaq day at $97.17, up 17% on the $83 IPO price, after touching $115. The close values the Claude maker near $1.76 trillion, while the Nasdaq fell 2.3% and other big tech stocks slid. After hours ANT dipped to about $92.
deck.whyItMatters: The first pure-play frontier lab now has a daily public price; a first day that held most of its gain while the rest of tech sold off gives AI lenders and investors a benchmark, but the fade from $115 shows how unsettled the AI trade is.
deck.checked: Closing price, change and volume checked on Nasdaq's own quote data (opened); day range from Yahoo Finance data; valuation and market moves from the BBC (opened)
deck.storyline: Storyline: Anthropic's money and IPO · day 26
deck.detailHtml:
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as ANT on 19 Nov. Nasdaq's own quote shows it closed at $97.17, up $14.17 or 17.1% on the $83 IPO price, with about 852 million shares traded; market data put the day's range at $92.72-$115.10. The BBC says the opening pop briefly took the company close to $2 trillion and the close values it at about $1.76 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable listed companies. The rest of tech did worse: the Nasdaq Composite fell about 2.3%, Alphabet 2.9% and Amazon about 3.9%. In after-hours trading ANT was at about $91.95 (-5.4%). The IPO itself, the largest ever at about $81bn, closes today (20 Nov).

A 17% first-day gain is modest by tech-IPO standards but large in money: about $250bn of value created on top of an offering already priced above its range. More telling is the shape of the day. ANT opened near $111, peaked at $115 and spent the afternoon falling while the Nasdaq dropped 2.3%, and it gave back another 5% after hours. Investors want exposure to frontier AI, but they are pricing it day by day.

For banks and lenders the useful number is not the pop but the new reference point. Data-centre loans, GPU-backed credit and private marks for other AI companies (OpenAI included) will now be compared with a listed, audited peer. The ECB warned the day before ANT listed that AI valuations rest on 'ambitious earnings expectations' and that debt-funded AI infrastructure could carry an equity correction into bond markets (see the ECB card).

deck.headline: Chase, Visa and Mastercard confirm vendor breaches after extortion gang claims them
deck.summary: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard confirmed breaches at outside vendors after the n0n extortion gang listed them. Chase says marketing data with some names and emails was reached; Mastercard says emails from one benefit programme leaked; Visa says no card numbers were affected. Expect targeted phishing.
deck.whyItMatters: No payment data is reported lost, but names and emails tied to bank and card brands are exactly what phishing crews need; expect lookalike 'security alert' emails, and note that all three exposures came through vendors, not the firms' own systems.
deck.checked: Company statements checked in The Register's report (opened); WSJ headline seen, not opened
deck.storyline: Storyline: big data breaches · day 5
deck.detailHtml: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard said on 19 Nov they are investigating breaches at outside service providers after the extortion group n0n, believed to be Russia-based, posted all three on its leak site on Monday. Chase said on X that attackers 'accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses', and that it is not linked to its outage earlier this week. Mastercard said a 'limited amount of email addresses' from a subset of cardholders in a specific benefit programme was exposed and contained. Visa said a provider in Asia Pacific was involved, its systems were not, and no card numbers were affected. None named the vendors. n0n appeared in September and listed 108 victims in its first month (The Register).

deck.headline: US approved 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China in six months, data shows
deck.summary: A House committee published licence data showing Commerce approved 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for Chinese firms between December and May, including 150,000 for Tencent and 75,000 for Alibaba, out of 3.4 million requested. All four named buyers are on the Pentagon's military list. Nvidia says it has stopped H200 shipments.
deck.whyItMatters: The release turns the Nvidia-Huang scandal into an enforcement fight; tighter licensing and foundry rules are likely, which matters for anyone financing data centres in Asia or exposed to Chinese cloud demand.
deck.checked: Figures checked in Al Jazeera's Reuters report (opened); committee statement quoted there, not opened
deck.storyline: Storyline: US limits on AI sales to China · day 6
deck.detailHtml: Committee chair Brian Mast used his powers under the Export Control Reform Act to publish licence data showing the Commerce Department approved exports of 879,000 advanced AI chips, Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X, to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, out of 3.4 million requested. Approvals included 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD; all four are on the Pentagon's list of Chinese military companies. It is not clear how many were shipped. Nvidia says approvals came with 'strict conditions and limited volumes' and that it 'has since stopped shipping H200s to China'. Separately, Samsung and TSMC have paused some China shipments under tightened foundry rules (Reuters, DigiTimes headlines).

deck.headline: VMware patches vCenter zero-day that Chinese hackers exploited for two months
deck.summary: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-severity vCenter flaw that gives unauthenticated attackers admin access. Mandiant says the China-linked Armory Castle group exploited it from early September, forging login tokens and planting backdoors. There is no workaround: patch to VMSA-2026-0009 and check for rogue admin accounts.
deck.whyItMatters: VCenter runs the virtual machines of most large banks; patch now, then hunt for unexpected SSO admin accounts and forged SAML tokens, because a two-month head start means some networks are already compromised.
deck.storyline: Storyline: critical patches to apply now · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Broadcom released emergency fixes on 19 Nov (VMSA-2026-0009) for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8), a flaw in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter Server that lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access get an administrator session. All vCenter versions before the fixed releases are affected, including inside VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation; there is no workaround. Google's Mandiant, which reported it, says the China-linked group Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) used it from early September: it got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, used a tool called Bonesaw to steal SAML signing material, created a single-sign-on admin account, forged tokens, installed backdoors and took the vCenter master encryption key before moving to ESXi hosts. The same advisory fixes four flaws in SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows.

deck.headline: ECB warns AI valuations and debt-funded data centres now threaten financial stability
deck.summary: The ECB's stability review says AI valuations rest on ambitious earnings hopes and that debt-funded AI infrastructure could carry an equity sell-off into bond markets. Euro-area banks are exposed through AI lending but judged resilient. Protos says the review counts about $4.5 trillion of off-balance-sheet tech commitments.
deck.whyItMatters: This is the supervisor telling banks to look at AI exposure as credit risk, not just equity risk: data-centre loans, GPU-backed lending and lending to non-banks that finance AI are the places it will ask about.
deck.storyline: Storyline: how AI gets financed · day 12
deck.detailHtml: The European Central Bank's twice-yearly Financial Stability Review, published on 18 Nov, puts AI valuations alongside fiscal imbalances and geoeconomic tension as the main risks. It says equity prices depend on 'ambitious earnings expectations' that financing worries or cheaper AI models could challenge, and that AI infrastructure is 'increasingly funded through debt, such that a potential change in sentiment could spread losses from equity markets to bond markets'. Euro-area banks and non-banks are exposed through AI financing and sovereign bonds; banks are judged well placed thanks to strong profits, capital and liquidity, with vulnerabilities larger in some non-banks. The issue also has a special focus on how AI is reshaping cyber threats. Protos reports the review counts about $4.5 trillion in debt-like off-balance-sheet commitments (data-centre leases, cloud and chip contracts) at eight US tech firms, up 287% on 2025.

deck.headline: Citi understated a European trading unit's risky assets by $35bn, Reuters reports
deck.summary: Reuters reports Citigroup misbooked trades at a European trading unit and understated its risk-weighted assets by about $35 billion. Citi says it found and fixed the capital-modelling issue this summer, the unit stayed above minimums and it injected capital. It is a setback in Citi's push to escape regulatory restrictions.
deck.whyItMatters: A capital-modelling error of this size is the kind of control failure supervisors have spent five years asking Citi to fix; it may delay the lifting of its consent orders.
deck.storyline: Storyline: bank capital and risk controls · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Citigroup incorrectly booked trades at a European trading subsidiary, understating its risk-weighted assets by about $35bn, two people told Reuters on 19 Nov. Citi said it 'identified and resolved an internal capital modeling issue' at the unit this summer; the subsidiary 'remained fully compliant with regulatory minimums throughout, with no impact on the holding company or main operating bank', and Citi 'injected capital to immediately' restore its buffers. Reuters calls it a setback for CEO Jane Fraser, who has been trying to get regulators to lift long-running restrictions tied to the bank's risk and data controls.

deck.headline: UN's top court finds Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a first for any state
deck.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled 9-6 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the first time any state has been found guilty of genocide by an international court. The 2017 crackdown killed thousands and drove over 700,000 people into Bangladesh. The ruling will shape the Gaza case.
deck.whyItMatters: The ruling sets the legal bar other genocide cases, including South Africa's against Israel, will be measured against, and raises sanctions and compliance risk for anyone dealing with Myanmar's military.
deck.storyline: Storyline: international courts and war crimes · day 1
deck.detailHtml: The International Court of Justice found on 19 Nov that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time an international court has found a state guilty of genocide. The vote was 9-6. Court president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the 'intention to destroy' a substantial part of the Rohingya and engaged in 'extensive destruction of evidence'; the court found genocidal intent 'the only reasonable inference'. The 2017 military crackdown killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee; about a million refugees live in camps in Cox's Bazar. The Gambia brought the case; Myanmar denied it. The NYT says the ruling sets up the court's fight over Israel and Gaza.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules · Al Jazeera: world reacts · NYT: ruling sets up court fight over Israel and Gaza

deck.headline: European Commission confirms an AI-run cyberattack took staff systems offline for days
deck.summary: The European Commission confirmed an 'AI-generated cyber campaign' detected on 22 October that knocked payroll, leave and other staff systems offline for over 10 days. Politico says investigators found the open-source AI hacking platform ARTEX. The Commission says there was no broad data breach and no ransom demand.
deck.whyItMatters: A major institution has now confirmed an attack run largely by an off-the-shelf AI tool; banks' incident plans should assume this speed and volume of probing, and check exposure of HR and payroll systems.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI in cyberattacks · day 22
deck.detailHtml: Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed on 19 Nov that the European Commission was hit by what he called an 'AI-generated cyber campaign', first detected on 22 Oct. Politico, which broke the story, says CERT-EU found the attackers used ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform the FBI warned last week is used by criminals and state groups. Personnel services, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation, were disrupted for more than 10 days. The Commission says it took services offline as a precaution, notified affected people, found no evidence of a broad breach of staff data and knows of no ransom demand. It did not explain why it did not disclose the attack earlier.

deck.headline: Ruby2Shell flaw lets attackers take over stock Rails apps without logging in
deck.summary: Veria Labs disclosed Ruby2Shell, a flaw that lets attackers run code on default Rails and Sinatra apps without logging in. Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10. Self-hosted GitLab and GitHub Enterprise Server had no fix yet on 20 November.
deck.whyItMatters: Self-hosted GitLab and GitHub Enterprise sit at the heart of bank software delivery; restrict their network exposure until vendor patches land, and upgrade Ruby everywhere else.
deck.storyline: Storyline: critical patches to apply now · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Veria Labs disclosed Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825), a bug in Ruby's handling of strings in legacy encodings that gives remote code execution without authentication on apps built with Rails or classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Fixed Ruby releases are 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10; every release back to 2.4 is affected. Products that bundle their own Ruby need vendor fixes: as of 20 Nov Veria lists GitLab (19.6.0 and earlier), GitHub Enterprise Server (3.22.5 and earlier) and Chatwoot as still vulnerable, and Mastodon, OpenProject and Discourse as patched.

deck.headline: Daily pill halts tumour growth in 90% of advanced pancreatic cancer patients in trial
deck.summary: In an early trial, the daily pill daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy stopped tumour growth in about 90% of 61 people with advanced pancreatic cancer and made tumours undetectable on scans in one in 12. Cancer Research UK calls it the biggest advance in decades; doctors say it is not a cure.
deck.whyItMatters: Pancreatic cancer has the worst survival of common cancers; a drug that 'drugs the undruggable' RAS target would reshape oncology pipelines and pharma valuations if late-stage trials confirm it.
deck.storyline: Storyline: new medicines · day 5
deck.detailHtml: In an early trial of daraxonrasib, a daily pill that targets the RAS proteins behind most pancreatic cancers, given with chemotherapy to 61 people recently diagnosed with advanced, spread disease, tumours stopped growing in about 90%, shrank or disappeared in just over 60%, and became undetectable on CT scans in about 8% (one in 12), the BBC reports. Patients were followed for about a year and a half on average. Cancer Research UK called it 'the biggest leap forward in decades'; Memorial Sloan Kettering's Dr Wungki Park called the results extremely encouraging. Doctors stress it is not a cure and larger, longer studies are needed. Separately, New Scientist reports a virus injection halted pancreatic cancer in three patients.

deck.headline: Anthropic details how Claude solved two open black-hole physics problems, with preprints
deck.summary: Anthropic published two preprints showing Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open black-hole physics problems: finishing a 20-year-old holography calculation and finding the exact limit of a test for quantum-gravity theories. The results are not yet peer reviewed; physicists' checks are the real test.
deck.whyItMatters: A frontier lab is now publishing checkable research results, not just benchmark scores; watch whether physicists confirm them, since that is the real test of 'AI scientist' claims.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI for science · day 20
deck.detailHtml: Anthropic published a detailed post and two preprints on 19 Nov describing how Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics, both about black holes and quantum gravity. First, it completed a calculation physicists set up more than 20 years ago in holographic duality, showing that a sudden transition associated with black-hole formation persists even where spacetime has no definite shape. Second, it found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate quantum-gravity theories. The results were first mentioned at Fable 5.2's launch on 10 Nov; this is the first full account. The claims have not yet been peer reviewed.

deck.headline: UK tribunal forces government to admit its secret order to break Apple's encryption
deck.summary: A UK tribunal ruled the government must admit it served Apple a secret order demanding access to encrypted iCloud data, rejecting national-security objections. Apple had withdrawn its strongest iCloud encryption in the UK rather than comply, and welcomed the ruling.
deck.whyItMatters: Secret backdoor orders are the biggest legal risk to end-to-end encryption that banks and their customers rely on; a public record makes it harder for governments to demand them quietly.
deck.storyline: Storyline: privacy fines on big tech · day 2
deck.detailHtml: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on 19 Nov that the UK government must confirm it served Apple a secret technical capability notice demanding access to encrypted customer data, rejecting the Home Office's argument that disclosure would damage national security (TechCrunch). The original order reportedly sought access to users' data worldwide; Apple refused and withdrew its Advanced Data Protection iCloud encryption for UK users. The order was later narrowed to British nationals, and Apple challenged that too. Apple, previously barred from even confirming the order, said it welcomes the decision.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGTechCrunch: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor orderAGGREGATORMacanorak (HN 475 points)

deck.headline: Gemini for Mac can now operate desktop apps and websites on your behalf
deck.summary: Google's Gemini app for Mac can now operate desktop apps and websites for you, clicking and typing in a background window while you keep working. It pauses for logins and payments. Developers also get Tool Retrieval, which loads agent tools on demand to save tokens.
deck.whyItMatters: Desktop agents that operate any app, including banking portals, are arriving on staff laptops; the 'pause for logins and payments' design is the control to look for, and the one Citi-style liability terms assume.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI agents for consumers · day 10
deck.detailHtml: Google's Gemini app for Mac now has computer use: it can click, type and fill in forms across local desktop apps and the web, working in an 'isolated background window with a live preview' so the user keeps their own screen and cursor. Users choose which apps it may use and can stop it with one click; it pauses for logins and payments and asks before sensitive actions. Google's examples include batch colour-grading photos and copying details from local PDFs into forms. For developers, Google launched Tool Retrieval in preview in the Gemini Interactions API, which loads tool definitions only when needed to cut tokens and keep tool choice accurate as agents grow.

deck.headline: MoonPay applies for a US trust bank charter to issue stablecoins
deck.summary: MoonPay applied to the OCC for a national trust bank charter to issue and redeem stablecoins and hold digital assets, taking no deposits and making no loans. It joins a queue of crypto and payments firms seeking federal charters before the GENIUS Act takes effect on 18 January.
deck.whyItMatters: The queue of crypto and payments firms seeking federal charters means banks will soon compete with OCC-supervised stablecoin issuers for corporate treasury and payments business.
deck.storyline: Storyline: banks and stablecoins · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Crypto payments firm MoonPay has applied to the OCC for a national trust bank charter, an OCC filing shows. MoonPay National Trust Bank, based in Miami Beach, would offer stablecoin issuance and redemption, reserve management and digital-asset custody under federal supervision, but would not take deposits or make loans. MoonPay already provides white-label stablecoin infrastructure for businesses. The filing comes before the GENIUS Act takes effect on 18 Jan 2027, setting federal rules on stablecoin reserves and redemption; Rain, Modern Treasury and others have also applied for trust charters (Cointelegraph).

deck.headline: Commonwealth Bank gives away the AI tool it uses to find security bugs in code
deck.summary: Commonwealth Bank released CodeCheck, a free AI harness based on its own internal tooling that steers Codex or Claude Code to find security flaws before code ships. It runs on the user's systems and CBA sees nothing. The bank warns it can miss bugs and raise false alarms.
deck.whyItMatters: A big bank is publishing the AI security workflow it trusts internally, a practical template for any bank's engineering teams and a sign that AI code review is becoming standard control practice.
deck.storyline: Storyline: how banks put AI to work · day 4
deck.detailHtml: Commonwealth Bank of Australia released CodeCheck by CommBank on 18 Nov, a free cyber-security tool and AI harness built by its security engineers from a capability used in the bank's own development process. It is designed for businesses writing code with AI agents OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code: it guides the agent to look for vulnerabilities before code reaches production and returns the risk details and supporting evidence to the engineer. It runs inside the user's own environment, and CBA says it has no access to their code or findings. Users still pay for their AI agent and model. CBA cautions it can miss vulnerabilities and flag safe code, and calls it a one-time open release.

deck.headline: Insurer Arbol launches cover against GPUs losing value faster than planned
deck.summary: Arbol launched parametric insurance that pays out if a benchmark GPU rental index falls below an agreed level, aimed at lenders, lessors and cloud firms holding GPUs as assets. Separately, Allianz Commercial warns AI losses are hiding inside cyber, D&O and liability policies.
deck.whyItMatters: GPU-backed loans have no long price history; a tradable hedge on GPU rental rates gives lenders a way to cap collateral risk, and its pricing will reveal what insurers think AI chips are worth in three years.
deck.storyline: Storyline: insuring AI risks · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Arbol, a parametric underwriter, launched GPU Residual Value Protection on 19 Nov for anyone carrying GPU value on its books: hyperscalers, neoclouds and other compute owners, plus lessors, lenders and residual-value guarantors. Because it is parametric, it pays cash at the end of the term if a benchmark GPU rental index falls below a strike level the client picks, rather than after a loss assessment (Artemis). Separately, Allianz Commercial warns that confirmed AI claims understate true exposure because most AI losses are absorbed into cyber, D&O and product-liability policies (Insurance Business).

deck.headline: India may delay UPI merchant fees past 2027 polls, hitting Paytm and Pine Labs
deck.summary: India may delay a planned 0.4% merchant fee on larger UPI payments until after the 2027 state elections because the government fears a merchant backlash. Shares of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik fell up to about 9-11% as the expected fee income for payment firms recedes.
deck.whyItMatters: UPI handles most Indian retail payments for free; without MDR, banks and payment apps keep subsidising it, and Indian fintech valuations that assumed a fee stream need resetting.
deck.storyline: Storyline: India's payment licences · day 2
deck.detailHtml: The introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on some UPI payments could be pushed beyond the 2027 elections in five states, Financial Express reports (via Inc42), because the government fears a backlash from merchants; the government, RBI and NPCI have not agreed a start date. The proposed framework charges 0.4% on eligible merchant payments above Rs 2,000, capped at Rs 300 per transaction. Shares of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik fell sharply on 19 Nov: Reuters says they 'plunged', Mint puts the drop at up to 9% and some reports say Paytm lost nearly 11%.

deck.headline: Houthi attack damages Riyadh tower housing Saudi wealth fund as Hormuz tanker strikes rise
deck.summary: A Riyadh skyscraper housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund was damaged as the kingdom reported new Houthi attacks. Iranian strikes on Hormuz tankers have also intensified, with two seafarers missing this week, even though Brent crude has fallen about a fifth this month.
deck.whyItMatters: Attacks reaching the Saudi capital's financial district raise the war-risk premium on Gulf assets even as oil falls; shipping and energy-insurance costs, not crude prices, are the channel to watch.
deck.storyline: Storyline: the Iran war and the economy · day 9
deck.detailHtml: A skyscraper in Riyadh that houses the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund was damaged on 19 Nov, witnesses said, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis (Reuters via The Japan Times); Al Jazeera reports attacks also on Jizan. Oil has moved the other way: Brent fell about a fifth this month as Middle East exports neared pre-war levels and the IEA said supply now outpaces demand.

deck.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin sign a nuclear-war statement that skips Ukraine and Iran
deck.summary: Trump, Xi and Putin ended their first three-way summit with a declaration that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought', plus priorities on UN reform and oil supplies. It does not mention the Ukraine or Iran wars and sets no arms-cut framework. Analysts call it mostly symbolic.
deck.whyItMatters: Markets got optics, not a deal; the oil-supply language and any follow-up arms talks are the parts with real consequences.
deck.update: The summit ended with a joint statement that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought', but nothing on Ukraine or Iran
deck.storyline: Storyline: the Trump, Xi and Putin summit · day 3
deck.detailHtml: The first summit between the leaders of the three biggest nuclear powers ended on 19 Nov with a declaration affirming that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought', the same wording the five UN Security Council members used before. It lists priorities including UN reform, oil supplies and diplomatic immunity, but does not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran and sets no denuclearisation framework. The talks lasted about 1 hour 20 minutes; Xi said nuclear weapons should eventually be 'completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed', and Putin spoke of a 'mutual understanding'. Analysts called it mostly symbolic (Guardian). Trump also said he and Xi want 'moderate' AI rules (Reuters headline).

deck.headline: California subpoenas Nvidia over whether China got chips or secrets after Huang scandal
deck.summary: California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia to examine whether the company or former CEO Jensen Huang let China obtain advanced chips or secrets, and whether investors were misled. Nvidia shares are down 22% since the scandal broke, and a separate lawsuit targets Alibaba's ties to the suspected spy.
deck.whyItMatters: Nvidia now faces a state securities probe on top of federal and congressional scrutiny; disclosure risk, not demand, is driving the stock.
deck.update: California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia over whether China obtained chips or secrets and investors were misled
deck.storyline: Storyline: who runs Nvidia · day 8
deck.detailHtml: California Attorney General Rob Bonta served Nvidia an investigative subpoena on 19 Nov, probing whether the company's or former CEO Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, which could break California law if investors and the public were misled. 'Companies cannot mislead their investors,' Bonta said. Huang left after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of spying for China; Nvidia shares have fallen 22% since early November, and its board says it will not reinstate him (BBC). A shareholder suit also accuses Alibaba of hiding ties to the suspected spy (CNA headline). The House committee's chip-licence release (see above) adds pressure.

alsoToday.headline: FDIC spells out which fintech fees make partner deposits count as brokered
alsoToday.summary: An FDIC proposal dated 17 Nov implements a provision of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that lets eligible banks with under $10bn in assets exclude certain custodial deposits from brokered-deposit totals. Fees tied to deposit volume or accounts opened would count as paying for deposits and fall outside the exception, but a bank could pay a fintech separately for recordkeeping…
alsoToday.whyItMatters: For community banks running banking-as-a-service, the fee structure in partner contracts now decides whether the deposits count as brokered.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: banks and their fintech partners · day 1
alsoToday.detailHtml: An FDIC proposal dated 17 Nov implements a provision of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that lets eligible banks with under $10bn in assets exclude certain custodial deposits from brokered-deposit totals. Fees tied to deposit volume or accounts opened would count as paying for deposits and fall outside the exception, but a bank could pay a fintech separately for recordkeeping (PYMNTS).
alsoToday.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGPYMNTS: FDIC proposal details how banks can pay fintechs in deposit deals

alsoToday.headline: Securities watchdogs urge immediate quantum preparations, warning upgrades will slow blockchains
alsoToday.summary: The International Organization of Securities Commissions said on 19 Nov firms should start preparing for quantum threats now because migration will take years. Its report warns that some quantum-resistant signatures are much larger than today's, so fewer transactions fit in each block; a test version of Solana ran about 90% slower.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Post-quantum migration is moving from a security-team topic to a markets-regulator expectation, with real performance costs for tokenised assets.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: preparing finance for quantum computers · day 1
alsoToday.detailHtml: The International Organization of Securities Commissions said on 19 Nov firms should start preparing for quantum threats now because migration will take years. Wallets that keep older keys could remain exposed (Cointelegraph; Reuters says IOSCO urged 'immediate action' on quantum risks to finance).

alsoToday.headline: Merck signs Isomorphic Labs to design cancer drugs with AI
alsoToday.summary: Merck and Isomorphic Labs said on 19 Nov they will collaborate to discover small-molecule candidates for an undisclosed oncology target (STAT). Terms were not disclosed. It follows Isomorphic's $5bn Series C last week; Medical Daily notes none of its candidates has yet been tested in animals or people.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Big pharma keeps paying for AI drug design before any AI-designed drug has proven itself in trials.

alsoToday.headline: FDA approves Sanofi's first drug for the brain symptoms of Gaucher disease
alsoToday.summary: The FDA approved Sanofi's Infilbray (venglustat) on 18 Nov for Gaucher disease type 3 in adults and children weighing at least 15kg. It is the first approved therapy for the disease's neurological symptoms, such as dementia and loss of muscle control; the small molecule crosses the blood-brain barrier and blocks an enzyme needed to make the fatty molecules that build up (MedCity…
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A first-in-class approval for a rare brain disease, a week ahead of its 25 Nov target date.

alsoToday.headline: Japan's core inflation edges up to 2.2%, keeping a December BOJ hike in play
alsoToday.summary: Japan's core CPI rose 2.2% year on year in October, after 2.1% in September and just below the 2.3% forecast; the index excluding fresh food and fuel also rose 2.2%, after 2.4% (Reuters via CNA).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: With the Fed also leaning towards a December hike, the dollar is heading for a fourth weekly gain; yen funding costs and Asian chip stocks are where the pressure shows.

alsoToday.headline: Apple job listing reveals plans for its own Siri-linked AI agent
alsoToday.summary: An Apple job listing seeks engineers to build an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps and call services (The Verge); other reports say it would also write code and use sub-agents, linked to Siri.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: An agent built into a billion devices would set the default for how consumers let AI act on their accounts.

alsoToday.headline: Hong Kong regulator flags Hyperliquid as an unlicensed crypto platform
alsoToday.summary: Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission added Hyperliquid, the largest decentralised perpetual-futures exchange, and 'Hyperliquid Hong Kong' to its Alert List, saying it has no local licence and may have promoted trading services to Hong Kong investors (Cointelegraph).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Regulators are starting to treat big DeFi venues as exchanges, which matters for banks offering crypto access.

alsoToday.headline: Coinbase plans its own prediction markets in 2027, taking on partner Kalshi
alsoToday.summary: Coinbase plans to offer its own event contracts to US retail and institutional customers in the first half of 2027, Bloomberg reports (via PYMNTS). It now offers prediction markets through Kalshi and agreed in December 2025 to buy The Clearing Company.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Prediction markets are becoming a mainstream brokerage product while states and courts still fight over who regulates them.

alsoToday.headline: Hormuz tanker attacks intensify even as oil prices slide a fifth
alsoToday.summary: Attacks on oil tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz picked up in October and have continued at a higher tempo this month, according to Bloomberg data; at least two seafarers are missing after attacks this week.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: An analyst calls it 'something like a war, but not exactly a war'; marine war-risk premiums, not crude, carry the cost.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: the Iran war and the economy · day 9
alsoToday.detailHtml: Attacks on oil tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz picked up in October and have continued at a higher tempo this month, according to Bloomberg data; at least two seafarers are missing after attacks this week. alsoToday.headline: Violence flares in Bangladesh ahead of Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile
alsoToday.summary: Violent protests and killings have broken out in Bangladesh ahead of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile in India, the Guardian reports; France 24 shows her supporters vandalising a ruling-party office, and other reports say border-guard platoons were sent to her hometown, Gopalganj.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Unrest in the world's second-largest garment exporter is a supply-chain and sovereign-credit risk to watch into December.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Violent protests and killings have broken out in Bangladesh ahead of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile in India, the Guardian reports; France 24 shows her supporters vandalising a ruling-party office, and other reports say border-guard platoons were sent to her hometown, Gopalganj. Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia in November 2025, says she will return in December; officials say she will be arrested.

alsoToday.headline: Trump posthumously pardons baseball hits king Pete Rose
alsoToday.summary: Donald Trump gave a 'Complete and Total Pardon' to the late Pete Rose on 19 Nov. Rose, who died in 2024 aged 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns and was banned from MLB for betting on games; MLB reinstated him posthumously last year, making him eligible for the Hall of Fame (BBC).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Symbolic, but it adds to the Hall of Fame debate as voting approaches.

alsoToday.headline: GTA VI makes over $2.3bn in its first day
alsoToday.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI made more than $2.36bn in under 24 hours after going live at midnight on 19 Nov, Sensor Tower told Deadline, with pre-order revenue above $2bn, making it 2026's best-selling game on pre-orders alone.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The biggest entertainment launch ever is a test of console networks and of Take-Two's earnings guidance.
